items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to the prohibition of commissions and rebates
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S6704

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to
the prohibition of commissions and rebates

 PURPOSE :

This bill clarifies that providing a benefit with the intention to
compensate or offer compensation, directly or indirectly, for any past
or present placement for a particular piece of title insurance
business by a title insurance corporation or agent or a representative
thereof is a prohibited illegal inducement under the Section 6409(d)
of the Insurance Law.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1: This section amends subdivision 2 of section 6409(d) of the
Insurance Law, clarifying that a marketing activity or conveyed
benefit or consideration shall be considered an illegal "inducement"
under this section if it is given with the intention to directly or
indirectly compensate a present or perspective client for any past or
present placement of title insurance business.

Section 2: Provides that this bill shall take effect immediately.

 JUSTIFICATION :

In 2017, as part of proposed rulemaking to clarify and enforce
Insurance Law Section 6409(d), the Department of Financial Services
drafted regulations that deemed any marketing practices that conveyed
a benefit onto a perspective client an illegal inducement "regardless
of whether provided as a quid pro quo for perspective business." This
interpretation goes beyond the intended scope of the law, and seems to
be an about face from previous guidance by the Office of General
Counsel (OGC), which were requested by and relied upon by the title
insurance industry, and which expressly required the presence of a
"quid pro quo" in order to constitute an illegal inducement. See i.e.
OGC Opinion No. 11-06-05 (June 21, 2011).

Because the title insurance industry does not engage in direct to
consumer advertising, insurers and agents need to be able to market
themselves and their services to their clients, including attorneys
and other real estate professionals, and they should be able to do
this in a way similar to others in the insurance industry and general
economy, as long as there is no direct or indirect "quid pro quo" for
the placement of a particular piece title insurance business. This
bill clarifies that the mere presence of common marketing activities
absent a quid pro quo does not constitute an illegal inducement under
6409(d).

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None to the state.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

summary: Relates to the definition of the phrase "an inducement for, or as compensation for, any title insurance business" as it relates to the prohibition against certain actions.
